Passage.summary: Neuroscience finding the causes of behavior in the brain cannot justify a fundamental change in legal responsibility and punishment, because the law requires only a minimum capacity for rational action, which people generally possess.

c1.text: The law assumes that people generally have the ability to make rational choices.

c2.text: To be exempt from legal responsibility, it must be proven that the defendant lacks the capacity for rational action.

c3.text: The capacity for rational action refers to the ability to act in ways that achieve one's desires based on one's own beliefs.

c4.text: The law is not concerned with whether people possess metaphysical free will, but only whether they meet the minimum standard of rationality.

c5.text: Neuroscience has not shown that people in general do not meet the minimum standard of rationality.

c6.text: Neuroscience finding the causes of behavior in the brain cannot justify a fundamental change in the practice of holding people legally responsible and punishing them.

h1.text: Human beliefs or desires play no role in causing behavior.

h2.text: Humans lack the capacity for rational action.

h3.text: Neuroscience can justify a fundamental change in the practice of legal responsibility and punishment.

a.note: If beliefs/desires cause no behavior, rational action is impossible, undermining premise c1 and rebutting c6.

h4.text: The capacity for rational action in humans arises from biological properties of evolved brains.

h5.text: Neuroscience can justify a fundamental change in the practice of legal responsibility and punishment.

b.note: The naive inference rb1 (biological origin of rational action negates responsibility) is undercut by c4: the law does not require metaphysical free will, only the capacity for rational action.

h6.text: A large proportion of people who committed crimes share common neural mechanisms that cause criminal behavior.

h7.text: Many offenders may lack the capacity for rational action at the time of the crime.

c.note: Common neural mechanisms among offenders do not provide an argument for c6, and may instead support exemptions under c2; therefore, c6 is not strengthened.
